concepts.name: Entities and attributes
concepts.summary: Identify the real-world entities in a set of requirements and the attributes that describe each one.

concepts.name: Tables, rows and columns
concepts.summary: Recognise that a relational schema stores each kind of thing in a table whose rows are records and whose columns are typed attributes.

concepts.name: Primary keys
concepts.summary: Explain that a primary key uniquely identifies each row and must be unique and never null.

concepts.name: Foreign keys
concepts.summary: Explain that a foreign key stores another table's key value to link rows across tables.

concepts.name: Relationship cardinality
concepts.summary: Distinguish one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships between entities.

concepts.name: Redundancy and anomalies
concepts.summary: Describe how repeating the same facts in many rows leads to inconsistencies when data is changed.

misconceptions.text: A database table is just like a spreadsheet, so putting everything into one wide table is fine.
A primary key must be a single meaningful value like a name or email.
A foreign key is just a column with the same name as another table's column.

concepts.name: Entity-relationship diagrams
concepts.summary: Draw an ER diagram from a requirements description showing entities, attributes and relationships with cardinality.

concepts.name: Natural versus surrogate keys
concepts.summary: Compare keys derived from real data with generated identifiers and pick one for simple cases.

concepts.name: Column data types
concepts.summary: Choose suitable data types for columns such as exact decimals for money, dates for dates and text lengths.

concepts.name: Basic column constraints
concepts.summary: Apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints to enforce simple rules in the schema.

concepts.name: First normal form
concepts.summary: Remove repeating groups and multi-valued columns so each cell holds one atomic value.

concepts.name: Junction tables
concepts.summary: Resolve a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships using a junction table, including attributes of the relationship.

concepts.name: Mapping ER to tables
concepts.summary: Translate an ER diagram into tables with keys and foreign keys placed on the correct side of each relationship.

misconceptions.text: Storing a comma-separated list of IDs in one column is a fine way to model a many-to-many relationship.
In a one-to-many relationship the foreign key goes on the 'one' side.
Prices are best stored in floating-point columns.

concepts.name: Functional dependencies
concepts.summary: Identify which attributes determine others in a table and use that to find candidate keys.

concepts.name: Second and third normal form
concepts.summary: Detect partial and transitive dependencies in a table and decompose it into 2NF and 3NF.

concepts.name: Boyce-Codd normal form
concepts.summary: Decide whether every determinant is a candidate key and decompose when it is not.

concepts.name: Referential actions
concepts.summary: Select cascade, restrict or set-null behaviour for foreign keys according to the lifecycle of the data.

concepts.name: Composite keys
concepts.summary: Use multi-column keys where the identity of a row depends on several attributes, and reference them correctly.

concepts.name: Index fundamentals for schemas
concepts.summary: Choose indexes for foreign keys and frequent filters, weighing read speed against write cost and storage.

concepts.name: Modeling hierarchies and optional data
concepts.summary: Represent trees, optional attributes and subtypes using self-referencing keys, nullable columns or separate tables.

misconceptions.text: A table with a single-column primary key is automatically in third normal form.
ON DELETE CASCADE is a safe default for every foreign key.
Adding an index to every column makes the database faster.

concepts.name: Lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition
concepts.summary: Evaluate a decomposition for whether it reconstructs the original data exactly and keeps constraints enforceable.

concepts.name: Higher normal forms
concepts.summary: Recognise multivalued and join dependencies and decide when fourth or fifth normal form is warranted.

concepts.name: Deliberate denormalization
concepts.summary: Judge when adding redundancy or summary data is justified by read patterns and how to keep it consistent.

concepts.name: Composite and covering indexes
concepts.summary: Design multicolumn, covering and partial indexes by assessing column order and query patterns.

concepts.name: Surrogate key trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate integer, UUID and natural keys regarding index size, locality, portability and uniqueness guarantees.

concepts.name: Temporal and history modeling
concepts.summary: Choose among versioned rows, effective-date ranges, audit tables and soft deletes to retain history.

concepts.name: Integrity beyond declared constraints
concepts.summary: Analyse rules that simple constraints cannot express and decide between triggers, deferred checks and application logic.

misconceptions.text: Denormalization is always a sign of poor design.
Any decomposition into smaller tables is safe as long as each table is in normal form.
A composite index on (a, b) serves queries filtering on b alone equally well.

concepts.name: Workload-driven schema evaluation
concepts.summary: Critique a schema against realistic read and write workloads, data volumes and growth, and prioritise changes by impact.

concepts.name: Schema evolution strategy
concepts.summary: Plan staged, backward-compatible schema migrations that avoid downtime and data loss on live systems.

concepts.name: Partitioning and sharding design
concepts.summary: Design partition or shard keys and schema layout that scale while keeping keys, constraints and joins workable.

concepts.name: Multi-tenant schema patterns
concepts.summary: Create a tenancy model by weighing shared tables, separate schemas and separate databases for isolation, cost and complexity.

concepts.name: Flexible and semi-structured columns
concepts.summary: Evaluate when JSON columns or EAV beat relational modeling and what integrity and query power is lost.

concepts.name: Relational versus analytical modeling
concepts.summary: Judge how transactional normalized designs differ from dimensional models and when each fits.

concepts.name: Design standards and governance
concepts.summary: Establish conventions, documentation and review practices so a team's schemas stay consistent and maintainable.

misconceptions.text: Storing everything in JSON columns removes the need for schema design.
Sharding is a free way to scale that leaves queries and constraints unchanged.
A star schema is just a more normalized version of the transactional schema.
